title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The authors ask three main questions: which technological breakthroughs enabled personalized tutoring, how current systems use real-time adaptation to improve engagement and academic performance, and what ethical challenges have emerged alongside these technologies. The review is motivated by persistent global learning gaps and interest in AI-based tools that can personalize instruction at scale.

The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The authors analyze tutoring systems through a four-part framework covering artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. They also conduct a latent class analysis that groups systems into three categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal tutoring systems that combine verbal, visual, and physical interaction. Across the reviewed studies, key AI techniques include Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, natural language processing, and large language models.

The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The included literature spans multiple learner groups, with examples and discussion prominently involving younger learners, middle school mathematics students, secondary physics learners, and some higher-education contexts. The review focuses primarily on students as end users of tutoring systems in educational environments, rather than on teachers or administrators as the main participants.

The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. Computer-based ITS are more scalable and cognitively adaptive, while robot-based systems are stronger for social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems integrating both approaches may offer the greatest educational benefit. They also conclude that important challenges remain, especially around scalability, data privacy, bias, transparency, and the still-limited cognitive adaptability of robotic systems.
